claims.text: The onset and progression of premelting and melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are governed by heterogeneous surface melting.
Local compositional fluctuations and defects depress the surface melting point relative to the bulk.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are solid and uniformly mixed, with a nominally homogeneous phase.
Standard high-energy synthesis produces the stated homogeneous initial condition.
The nanoparticles will be subjected to a controlled thermal ramp and a dwell slightly below the bulk melting point while being monitored in situ.
Nanoparticle size and dispersion will be held constant during heating in an inert atmosphere with controlled ramp rate and dwell time.
Surface defects and local compositional heterogeneities create surface regions with depressed melting temperatures.
Element segregation or surface imperfections lower the effective melting point at the nanoparticle surface relative to the interior.
Surface atoms become mobile and premelt before the nanoparticle core melts.
After surface melting begins, the liquid phase progressively propagates inward.
In situ characterization will reveal surface disordering and a liquid-like surface layer below the bulk melting point.
Melting will subsequently progress from the surface toward the particle interior.
The baseline nanoparticles remain fully solid and homogeneously ordered below the bulk melting threshold.
Oxidation, altered heating rates, or changes in nanoparticle size distribution could affect melting behavior.
The surface-melting initiation temperature depends on particle size and the degree of local compositional variation.
The magnitude of melting-point depression depends on particle size and local compositional variation.
Uniform melting with no early surface melting or compositional correlation would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe surface melting below the bulk melting point would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as uniformly mixed and homogeneous, while the proposed operative mediator requires pre-existing local compositional heterogeneities or segregation. The hypothesis does not explain how these heterogeneities coexist with, or emerge from, the stated homogeneous starting state.

The baseline is defined as nanoparticles remaining fully solid below the bulk melting threshold, whereas the prediction assigns a liquid-like surface layer to nanoparticles in that same temperature range. No distinct control population or treatment difference is specified to reconcile the two descriptions.
